title: Athena arms herself; the gates of heaven
intro: Athena exchanges her own woven robe for Zeus’ martial equipment. The aegis carries terrifying powers and images, making this an arming scene on a divine scale. Hera then drives the pair to obtain Zeus’ authorization.

notes.text: λέπαδνα are straps or pads of the harness associated with the yoke, not the reins held by the driver. δῆσε is aorist of δέω, ‘fastened.’ μεμαυῖα is feminine perfect participle of μέμονα, ‘eager,’ taking genitives ἔριδος and ἀϋτῆς, strife and battle-cry. The preparations have an explicitly combative purpose.

κατέχευεν is epic aorist of καταχέω, ‘poured / let fall.’ ἑανός here describes the soft or fine robe; ποικίλον adds its elaborate patterning. οὖδας is the ground or floor, dative οὔδει. Athena herself made and worked the garment: the scene begins by recalling her craft before displaying her warfare.

ἐνδῦσα is aorist active participle of ἐνδύω, ‘putting on,’ with Zeus’ tunic as object. θωρήσσετο is imperfect middle of θωρήσσω, ‘armed herself,’ with dative τεύχεσιν. δακρυόεντα agrees with πόλεμον, ‘tear-bringing war.’ The epithet keeps mortal suffering present amid the splendour of divine equipment.

αἰγίς is the aegis, a divine protective and terrifying object, worn here around the shoulders. θυσσανόεις means tasselled. ἐστεφάνωται is perfect middle/passive of στεφανόω, ‘is wreathed around,’ with Fear as subject. The description gives personified Panic, Strife, Strength, and chilling Pursuit a place on the object.

κρυόεις is chilling or freezing; Ἰωκή is pursuit or rout personified. Γοργείη means Gorgonian, qualifying the head of the monster (πέλωρον). τέρας is a portent or fearful sign. The aegis’ imagery is designed to overwhelm enemies, not merely decorate its bearer.

κυνέη is a helmet, whatever its original association with dogskin; this one is gold. ἀμφίφαλος and τετραφάληρος describe projections, bosses, or crests, whose exact physical reconstruction is uncertain. πρυλέεσσι are foot-soldiers. ἀραρυῖαν is feminine accusative perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω, ‘fitted,’ in the extravagant image of a helmet suited to the fighting men of a hundred cities.

βήσετο is an epic aorist middle of βαίνω in this narrative, ‘stepped,’ rather than a prediction. βριθύ, ‘heavy,’ and στιβαρόν, ‘stout,’ qualify the spear. δάμνησι is epic present subjunctive of δάμνημι, ‘subdue,’ in a general description of what she does with it. ὀβριμοπάτρη means daughter of a mighty father.

ἐπεμαίετο is imperfect of ἐπιμαίομαι, ‘reached at / plied,’ here using the whip. αὐτόμαται says the gates move of themselves. μύκον is imperfect of μύκω, ‘bellow, groan,’ giving them an audible opening. The Hours, Ὧραι, are their divine keepers, associated with ordered seasons and cosmic order.

ἐπιτέτραπται is perfect middle/passive of ἐπιτρέπω, ‘has been entrusted,’ with dative τῇς referring to the Hours. ἀνακλῖναι is aorist infinitive of ἀνακλίνω, ‘push back’; ἐπιθεῖναι is aorist of ἐπιτίθημι, ‘put in place.’ Opening and closing heaven is described as moving its dense cloud barrier. κεντρηνεκής characterizes horses responsive to the goad.

ἄτερ governs the separated genitive θεῶν … ἄλλων, ‘apart from the other gods.’ πολυδείρας means many-ridged, genitive πολυδειράδος. στήσασα is transitive aorist participle of ἵστημι, stopping the horses. ἐξείρετο, from ἐξείρομαι, means ‘questioned.’ Hera addresses Zeus at the highest summit before joining battle.
